title: Public-life engagement forms distinct participation styles rather than one civic ladder
source_unit: Pew Research Center Cross-Sectional Engagement Survey and American Trends Panel assignment to engagement groups

observations.period: July 9-December 5, 2025 survey; political interest by engagement group

denominator.unit: percent within Pew engagement groups assigned from 19 measures of political activity, civic involvement, religious attendance, and news attention

mobilizers_high_interest.unit: percent extremely or very interested in politics

observations.method: Pew cluster analysis of the Cross-Sectional Engagement Survey, with American Trends Panel respondents assigned to the resulting four groups; descriptive group comparison, not a participation treatment.
observations.uncertainty: Cluster labels depend on the selected 19 measures and survey period; the activity questions mostly refer to the prior 12 months, including the 2024 presidential election. Group membership is not a fixed identity or causal exposure.
observations.subgroup: Mobilizers, Connectors, Spectators, and Outsiders as defined by Pew; group shares and composition are source-specific.
observations.counterinterpretation: Political interest may help produce engagement, be produced by it, or reflect common causes such as education, identity, resources, information, or life stage.

observations.period: September 8-14, 2025 panel; trust in federal government and news by engagement group

denominator.unit: percent within Pew engagement groups in the American Trends Panel; source-specific trust response categories

federal_trust_mobilizers.unit: percent saying they can trust federal government just about always or most of the time

national_news_trust_mobilizers.unit: percent saying they have a lot or some trust in national news information

observations.method: Pew American Trends Panel estimates after assigning respondents to engagement groups based on the cross-sectional cluster solution; federal-government and news trust are kept as separate measures.
observations.uncertainty: These are cross-sectional group comparisons, not evidence that participation creates trust. Different question wording, nonresponse, survey mode, and assignment uncertainty apply to the two source surveys.
observations.subgroup: Four Pew engagement groups; national news trust values for Connectors and Spectators are 64% and 57%, respectively, and are retained in the detailed memo.
observations.counterinterpretation: Federal-government trust is low across all four groups, while news trust varies more; engagement does not translate into a general trust hierarchy.

observations.period: September 8-14, 2025 panel; perceived news fairness by engagement group

denominator.unit: percent within Pew engagement groups answering whether news organizations deal fairly with all sides or favor one side

news_favors_one_side_mobilizers.unit: percent saying news organizations tend to favor one side

observations.method: Pew engagement-group comparison of a normative/fairness judgment about news organizations; no objective content audit is implied.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived fairness is not news accuracy, bias coding, ownership, censorship, or exposure. The measure can reflect political identity, expectations, media use, and the distinction between watchdog and partisan roles.
observations.subgroup: Mobilizers, Connectors, Spectators, and Outsiders in the Pew panel assignment.
observations.counterinterpretation: High engagement can coexist with skepticism about fairness; distrust of news does not imply disengagement, and engagement does not imply institutional confidence.

related_sources.claim: Current Pew press-government legitimacy findings provide a complementary institutional-power and criticism-norm layer.
Current Pew AI-attitude findings provide a technology-concern and anticipated-work-change comparison.

boundary: This record describes engagement clusters and associated political, news, trust, and fairness judgments. It does not estimate a causal effect of civic participation, identify the same person's trigger-to-action path, measure objective news fairness, or establish that trust produces voting, organizing, switching, or non-use.
